            "Exactly. **We seed the world with a family of expressions, not a single ancestral phrase.** And every playthrough produces a different linguistic history.\n\nThat gives us two sources of diversity operating simultaneously:\n\n1. **Initial variation:** Different settlements begin with slightly different expressions, pronunciations, slang, and cultural attitudes.\n2. **Stochastic evolution:** Those variations change independently, interact, recombine, and occasionally spread across the subterranean world.\n\nAnd crucially, the initial distribution is itself randomized.\n\n### The founding vocabulary\n\nWe might begin with a pool like:\n\n- Well, fuck.\n- Oh, fuck.\n- We're fucked.\n- Fuck me.\n- Not again.\n- Well, shit.\n- Fucking hell.\n- This is fine.\n- For fuck's sake.\n- You've got to be fucking kidding me.\n\nThese expressions provide overlapping vocabulary, sounds, grammatical structures, and meanings.\n\nThen each civilization inherits a random subset, subject to its founding population and cultural ancestry.\n\n**We're not evolving ten independent catchphrases. We're evolving languages with a shared linguistic ancestry.**\n\n### And the simulation generates its own source material.\n\nSuppose a city survives three floods in 200 years.\n\nIts expression for impending disaster gradually becomes associated specifically with rising water.\n\nMeanwhile, a neighboring civilization experiences repeated collapses. Its corresponding expression develops associations with falling objects.\n\nCenturies later, the two populations merge.\n\nTheir languages interact, and the resulting civilization inherits both traditions.\n\nPerhaps they develop separate expressions for catastrophes involving water, falling rocks, and the especially regrettable combination.\n\nThe language engine doesn't need to know in advance what any of those expressions will become.\n\n### Here's the really important technical distinction\n\nI'd use a **seeded stochastic linguistic evolution engine**, with several interacting mechanisms:\n\n| Mechanism | Effect |\n|---|---|\n| Sound change | Pronunciations evolve |\n| Semantic drift | Meanings gradually change |\n| Grammatical change | Word order and structure evolve |\n| Borrowing | Connected cities exchange words |\n| Language contact | Populations develop mixed linguistic features |\n| Cultural selection | Memorable or socially important expressions spread |\n| Founder effects | Small isolated populations develop unusual variants |\n| Catastrophic disruption | Displacement accelerates language contact and divergence |\n\nAnd we should distinguish stochastic variation from unconstrained randomness.\n\nFor example, a sound change should generally operate across multiple words sharing the relevant phonetic environment, rather than randomly altering one word at a time.\n\nThat way, the results retain linguistic coherence even when they become unrecognizable.\n\n### One more entertaining consequence\n\nBecause each game's initial conditions and random             "Yes. **A contextual language-sampling mechanic.** And I think it could be considerably more interesting than conventional dialogue puzzles.\n\nRather than simply presenting the player with an unfamiliar sentence and demanding a translation, we let them **collect examples of a civilization's language in situations where they already know something about what's happening**.\n\nFor instance, you observe a city during a flood.\n\nA citizen shouts:\n\n> **“Vek taluma shen!”**\n\nA few turns later, during another flood:\n\n> **“Taluma! Taluma!”**\n\nThen you encounter a merchant discussing a damaged aqueduct:\n\n> **“Nesh taluma vek.”**\n\nYou begin to suspect *taluma* has something to do with water, flooding, or damage. You're not certain which.\n\nAnd importantly, you shouldn't necessarily be certain. Three observations might support several interpretations.\n\n### The Language Notebook 📖\n\nI'd give the player a notebook that automatically collects overheard expressions alongside contextual information.\n\nYou could highlight a word and assign a tentative meaning, compare examples, or look for related forms in neighboring civilizations.\n\nBut the game shouldn't simply tell you whether you're correct.\n\nInstead, you test your hypotheses through subsequent encounters.\n\n**The reward is improved understanding, not points for guessing vocabulary.**\n\n### The clever part: generating the text\n\nWe could use a lightweight grammatical system underlying each city's evolving expressions.\n\nIt would maintain a small vocabulary of concepts relevant to the simulation: water, food, danger, trade, shelter, authority, movement, possession, obligation, and so forth.\n\nThe game knows the intended meaning of each statement. It constructs that statement using the city's current vocabulary and grammatical conventions.\n\nThose conventions evolve stochastically alongside the vocabulary.\n\nSo we can generate genuinely new sentences rather than repeatedly presenting memorized phrases.\n\nFor example, the same city might produce:\n\n| Situation | Intended meaning | Generated utterance |\n|---|---|---|\n| Flood | Water is rising. | Vek taluma shen. |\n| Trade | We need food. | Nara sevek dun. |\n| Collapse | The ceiling is falling. | Kesh vuruma tal. |\n| Diplomacy | Do you bring food? | Nara dun sevek? |\n\n*These are illustrative placeholders, not output from a language engine.*\n\nThe important technical requirement is that the grammar and vocabulary remain consistent enough for the player to infer relationships.\n\nWe should also preserve historical forms, allowing you to consult old inscriptions when trying to interpret contemporary speech.\n\n### And there should be consequences for imperfect understanding.\n\nImagine you're negotiating passage through an unfamiliar city.\n\nYou understand approximately 40% of its language.\n\nThe governor makes a proposal.\n\nYou recognize the words for *water*, *three*, and *city*.\n\nYou confidently agree.\n\nYou have just promised to deliver three cities' worth of drinking water.\n\nYou don't own three cities.\n\nYou barely own a bucket.\n\nThe governor is delighted.\n\n**Your options are now diplomacy, bribery, or leaving before somebody produces a contract.**\n\nAnd the beautiful thing is that the entire encounter could arise from the world's existing circumstances.             "**Absolutely. That's a hard constraint on the language engine, not just a stylistic preference.**\n\nEvery language begins as English. Every subsequent form must be reachable through a historically and phonetically plausible sequence of changes.\n\nThat means we don't generate invented vocabulary and make it sound vaguely linguistic. We **evolve actual English vocabulary through sound changes, grammatical changes, and semantic shifts**.\n\nAnd critically, the game needs to remember how it got there.\n\n### How I'd implement it\n\n**1. Begin with spoken English, not English spelling.**\n\nThe underlying representation uses phonemes and phonological features. We can use the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) for inspection.\n\nFor example:\n\n*Well, fuck.* → /wɛl fʌk/\n\n**2. Apply plausible sound changes across a population's vocabulary.**\n\nChanges have phonetic environments and probabilities.\n\nFor example, a hypothetical lineage might undergo:\n\n| Stage | Change | Result |\n|---|---|---|\n| 0 | Ancestral English | /wɛl fʌk/ |\n| 1 | /w/ → /v/ | /vɛl fʌk/ |\n| 2 | /ʌ/ → /ə/ | /vɛl fək/ |\n| 3 | Intervocalic /l/ vocalization in a specified environment | No change here |\n| 4 | Final /k/ → /x/ | /vɛl fəx/ |\n\nThe example is deliberately modest. More dramatic divergence should accumulate through successive, individually plausible changes.\n\nWe shouldn't allow an arbitrary mutation simply because it produces an interesting-looking result.\n\n**3. Evolve grammatical structures independently.**\n\nLanguages don't evolve exclusively through phonetic drift.\n\nEnglish expressions might acquire new particles, develop habitual constructions, undergo reanalysis, or incorporate words from neighboring settlements.\n\nBut those additions must come from somewhere: inherited English vocabulary, productive derivation, attested earlier innovations within the simulation, or borrowing from another evolving language.\n\n**4. Preserve linguistic genealogy.**\n\nEvery transformation is recorded.\n\nA player examining an unfamiliar expression could eventually reconstruct its ancestry:\n\nContemporary utterance → earlier dialect → ancestral dialect → English.\n\nImportantly, some transformations should affect entire sound classes rather than individual words. That's how we maintain recognizable historical linguistic relationships.\n\n### The distinction that makes the game work\n\nWe need two interacting systems:\n\n**Linguistic evolution:** Changes the language itself according to plausible historical mechanisms.\n\n**Contextual utterance generation:** Uses the current language to express events occurring in the game.\n\nSo when a city experiences a catastrophic flood, the generator doesn't invent a vaguely foreign-sounding sentence about flooding.\n\nIt constructs the intended message from that city's inherited, evolved vocabulary and grammar.\n\nA player who has been observing the civilization can potentially decipher it.\n\nAnd if two civilizations diverged 500 years ago, their languages should generally retain more similarities than civilizations separated for 3,000 years, although contact and rates of change can complicate that relationship.\n\n### One important additional requirement\n\n**The simulation must distinguish phonetic plausibility from historical plausibility.**\n\nA perfectly pronounceable sequence isn't necessarily a plausible descendant of a particular English expression.\n\nWe should therefore retain an explicit chain of changes, with each transformation checked against its phonetic environment and the language's evolving sound system.\n\nThis doesn't mean we're reconstructing a real future language. The particular sequence of innovations is stochastic, and our model will necessarily simplify historical linguistics.\n\nBut it means every generated language is intended to have a defensible *history*, not merely a convincing sound.\n\nAnd I'd make the linguistic engine entirely independent of the game's humor. The language evolves according to its own rules; the comedy comes from what people find themselves needing to say.\n\n**The player starts by understanding everyone perfectly. Centuries later, understanding anyone becomes an archaeological exercise.**\n\nAnd in principle, a sufficiently observant player could work backward through the sound correspondences and rediscover the English underneath."
